newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl regrets lack of progress at UN climate talks.
newsitem.headline: Kohl regrets lack of progress at UN climate talks.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl criticised the United States and Japan on Friday for blocking worldwide standards on cutting greenhouse gases and he pledged to keep up pressure for more environmental controls.

Kohl, reporting to parliament on the Denver G7 summit and the United Nations Earth Summit, said Germany and its European partners were determined to reach clear goals by the end of this year for reducing the gases that cause global warming.
Environmental groups blasted U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday for refusing at the U.N. Earth Summit to announce specific targets for cutting back fossil fuel emissions.

Clinton disappointed his European partners at the Group of Seven summit in Denver last week by blocking their plan to have the world's leading industrialised states pledge to cut their carbon emissions by 15 percent below 1990 levels by 2010.
"I regret that we did not succeed, this year at least, to convince the United States and Japan," Kohl told parliament.

"We cannot and will not give in on this point. I will work at the Climate Conference in Kyoto at the end of this year ... so that we reach agreements on a clear reduction of greenhouse gases by 2010."

Rudolf Scharping and Joschka Fischer, floor leaders of the opposition Social Democrats and the Greens respectively, criticised Kohl for campaigning for strict limits internationally while allowing greenhouse gas emissions in western Germany to rise since 1990.
Most of the reductions in German carbon emissions since 1990 have been the result of shutting down the heavily polluting factories in former communist East Germany.

Scientists say greenhouse gases from fossil fuels like coal or oil could raise atmospheric temperatures by as much as 3.3 degrees celsius (six degrees Fahrenheit), transforming the world's climate and raising sea levels significantly.

The European Union set a target of 15 percent cuts in greenhouse gases by 2010 at its Amsterdam summit this month. Prime Minister Tony Blair said in Denver that Britain aimed to cut its greenhouse gas emissions by 20 percent in 2010.

Clinton said the United States, the world's biggest polluter, said on Thursday the European target was impossible to meet but added that Washington would cut American greenhouse gas emissions significantly.
He also pledged one billion dollars in aid to help developing countries reduce their production of carbon dioxide and other gases harming the environment.
Clinton promised the United States would make a strong commitment to "realistic and binding limits" but named no target numbers.

The United States, with the world's biggest economy, accounts for 23 percent of global carbon emissions, followed by China with 13.9 percent and Russia with 7.2 percent. Germany accounts for 3.8 percent.
